text.p: The United States on Wednesday applauded a deal to forge a peaceful new relationship between NATO and Russia and said it appeared likely the pact could be signed in Paris later this month.

"I'm very encouraged by what I hear from Moscow," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said. But she cautioned that Washington was still awaiting details of the accord, finalised in Moscow on Wednesday morning.
"We still have to hear from (NATO) Secretary General (Javier) Solana once he gets to Brussels." She spoke at a State Department picture-taking session with Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.

The NATO-Russia pact was intended to forge closer ties between the alliance and its former enemy and was aimed at assuaging Russian concerns over the expansion of NATO eastwards to take in former members of the Warsaw Pact.
U.S. officials said the agreement would create a formal joint cooperation council and give Russia a voice but no veto in NATO decision-making on European security.
Rodionov, who spoke later at the Pentagon, hailed the agreement as good for U.S.-Russian relations.

"It demonstrates the intention of both sides to meet each other's interests, to find a compromise ... I think that the agreement suits both Russia and the United States of America. I think it's very good," he said.
One administration official told Reuters the deal "preserves NATO's institutions and in no way limits the alliance prerogatives."

He noted the alliance's repeated assertion that it has "no intention, no plan, no need for stationing forces or nuclear weapons on the territory of new members" and said: "We will need to upgrade infrastructure (in new member states) to NATO standards and assure interoperability of equipment and weapons systems and there are no limits on that."

The text of the deal was agreed between Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov after months of tough negotiations between the two former Cold War foes. Details were not immediately released.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said "We're obviously very encouraged." He said the prospective agreement was something that President Bill Clinton had fought for and worked hard on "for quite some time."

"The president at Helsinki cleared the way for a lot of the issues that needed to be discussed," McCurry said, referring to Clinton's summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in the Finnish capital in March.

"It's looking likely if they can finalise this agreement that there would be a signing ceremony in Paris that President Yeltsin suggested occur," McCurry said. Yeltsin set a target of May 27 for a Paris big power summit to sign the agreement.

The announcement of the deal came in a joint statement from Moscow. U.S. officials did not have a chance to talk with Solana before he left Moscow and "so we don't know the substance" of the agreement, one official in Washington said.
McCurry said Solana would brief NATO representatives at alliance headquarters in Brussels on the agreement and Clinton was likely to make a public statement on Wednesday afternoon.

A breakthrough was blocked until now by a row over whether the pact should include written guarantees that NATO will not station military structures and nuclear arms on the territory of new member states. The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation has been reluctant to give such guarantees in writing.

Leaders of NATO's 16 countries meet in Madrid on July 8-9 to decide the alliance's first new members of the post-Cold War era. Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic are considered certain but Romania and Slovenia are also being discussed.
Moscow strongly opposed NATO expansion but agreed to negotiate a new relationship with the alliance after the United States and other NATO members made clear they would pursue enlargement anyway.
